request: Explain this change to developers who rely on the preview server.
context:
Why the preview server stopped watching everything
By the Lantern Tools maintainers

For most of its life, Lantern's preview server treated a project directory as a promise: anything underneath it might affect the page. It watched source files, downloaded packages, generated thumbnails, editor recovery files and the output of other tools. This was easy to explain and surprisingly difficult to live with. A photo import could trigger hundreds of rebuild requests even when no page referred to the imported folder.

The trouble was not simply the number of files. Some tools write a temporary file and rename it; others replace an entire directory. Our watcher sometimes interpreted each intermediate step as a separate meaningful change. Debouncing helped during steady streams of writes, but it also made small edits feel slower. Extending the delay further would have traded one annoyance for another.

In version 0.18, the preview server starts with three watched locations: the source directory, the public-assets directory and the project configuration file. It then adds files discovered through imports. Generated output is excluded even if it sits inside one of those locations. A rebuild still follows changes to an imported stylesheet outside the source directory, because the import establishes that dependency explicitly.

There is an important exception. A template that constructs a filename at runtime does not leave an import for the server to follow. Projects that load files this way need to list the containing directory in the new watch.extra setting. This setting accepts project-relative directories, not individual glob patterns. The example project includes a recipes directory because its pages look up recipe text by slug. Without that entry, editing the text will not refresh an already open preview.

We tried the change on eight internal projects. Six stopped rebuilding after unrelated asset-generation jobs. The other two showed little difference because their directories were already small. These observations are useful, but they are not a general performance benchmark. Network drives, unusually large dependency graphs and editors with different save behavior may produce different results.

The first release keeps an escape hatch: watch.mode can be set to broad, restoring the previous behavior. We expect to retain it through the next two minor releases. Removing it later depends on whether explicit dependencies cover the workflows people actually use; that decision has not been made.

After upgrading, edit a normal source file and then any content files your templates discover dynamically. If the second edit does not refresh the page, add its directory to watch.extra or temporarily use broad mode. Please include the relevant directory layout when reporting a missed update. A report that says only that watching stopped leaves us guessing about the relationship the server failed to see.
content_checks: Describe the default watched locations and imported dependencies
Explain watch.extra for runtime-discovered files
Preserve the temporary broad-mode escape hatch and limited trial evidence

request: Write a clear team update from this review, including what remains unresolved.
context:
The stale mirror incident
A review from the fictional Pebble Build team

On Tuesday morning, several developers could download an older release of our internal formatting package but not the version listed in the shared lockfile. The package service itself was healthy. The failure occurred at a regional mirror that had stopped accepting new objects overnight while continuing to serve objects it already held. Because ordinary availability checks requested an old package, the mirror looked healthy.

The first report arrived at 09:12. A developer had recreated a workspace and saw a missing-object response during installation. Colleagues with warm local caches could still build, which initially made the problem look specific to the new workspace. At 09:26, a second clean installation reproduced the failure. The team then compared requests through the mirror with direct requests to the package service and found the difference.

We routed affected clients around that mirror at 09:41. This restored downloads for the projects we checked. It also increased traffic to the main service, so we kept the bypass limited to the affected region. We found no evidence that existing package objects had changed. The incident concerned availability of new objects, not a detected modification of their contents.

The mirror's ingestion worker had filled its temporary directory. Completed transfers normally remove temporary files, but interrupted transfers left fragments behind. A cleanup job existed on the older mirror machines and had not been included in the configuration used for this replacement. The configuration review checked service startup and read access, but did not compare recurring maintenance jobs.

We removed the abandoned fragments, restored the cleanup job and verified that a newly published test package appeared at the mirror. Client routing returned to normal at 11:05. Those steps address the immediate failure. They do not by themselves tell us whether the cleanup policy is adequate for every interruption pattern or future traffic level.

Two follow-ups have owners. The infrastructure group will add temporary-directory usage to monitoring and document the maintenance jobs in the machine configuration. The developer-tools group will change the health probe so that it checks a recently published test object as well as a longstanding one. That probe needs care: a normal replication delay should produce a warning before it produces an outage alert. The acceptable delay has not yet been agreed.

We are also considering exposing mirror freshness in the client error message. This is a proposal rather than committed work, because the client currently cannot distinguish a delayed mirror from a genuinely absent package without making another request. We need to measure that extra request's cost before selecting a design.

The lesson from this incident is narrower than saying that caches are unreliable. A service can answer old questions correctly while failing to receive new information. Our checks measured whether the mirror could serve a package; the workflow depended on whether it could serve the package that had just become necessary.
content_checks: Explain why warm caches and old-object probes masked the failure
State the missing cleanup configuration and restoration
Distinguish owned monitoring work from unresolved delay and client-message proposals

request: Summarize the experiment for volunteers deciding whether to keep the booking system.
context:
What three repair afternoons taught us about reservations
Cedar Bench workshop report

Our monthly repair afternoon used to operate entirely by arrival order. The queue was easy to explain but difficult to predict. Someone with a loose cabinet handle might wait behind a radio that needed an hour of investigation. Visitors sometimes left without being seen, while a volunteer at a different table had nothing suitable to work on. We tested reservations to see whether knowing the mix of items ahead of time would help.

The trial covered three afternoons. Half of the available places could be reserved; the remaining half stayed open for walk-ins. A reservation was a place in the first assessment queue, not a promise of repair or a guaranteed finishing time. Visitors supplied an item description and chose either the first or second half of the afternoon. We did not ask them to diagnose the fault.

Descriptions helped us prepare. On the second afternoon, several visitors mentioned broken wooden joints, so we set up an extra clamping table. On the third, advance descriptions suggested more sewing work than our usual volunteer roster could handle. We contacted an additional sewing volunteer, who was able to attend. These were useful adjustments, although they depended on people being available.

Attendance was less straightforward. Across the trial, thirty places were reserved and twenty-four reservation holders arrived. Five people warned us they could not come; one did not. We offered canceled places to a short waiting list. A few walk-in visitors thought the event had become reservation-only because the new form was more prominent than the explanation beneath it. We corrected the sign for the final afternoon.

Volunteers recorded assessment waiting times when they remembered. The incomplete records suggest that the longest waits became shorter, but they do not support a reliable average or a precise comparison with previous months. We also ran with different numbers of volunteers each time. It would be misleading to attribute every change in the queue to the form.

There was a real administrative cost. One coordinator spent roughly forty minutes before each session checking descriptions, responding to questions and managing cancellations. That work happened at home and was easy for the rest of us to overlook. Keeping reservations means sharing that task or accepting that the system depends on one person's spare time.

Our proposal is to continue for two more afternoons with the same half-reserved, half-walk-in balance. We would make the walk-in invitation equally prominent and rotate coordination between two volunteers. If nobody can take the second coordination slot, we recommend returning to arrival order while retaining the item-description board at the entrance. The board provided useful triage even without a reservation.

The decision is therefore about the whole arrangement, including its hidden work. A tidier queue is welcome, but a system that only functions through unrecorded effort is not yet a dependable improvement.

request: Turn this engineering article into a thread with a strong opening.
context:
Complete synthetic engineering article: The fast answer that arrived too late
By the fictional Merrow inference team

The first number we put on our new inference dashboard was tokens per second. It was easy to collect and easy to celebrate. It also missed the complaint we heard most often from people using our assistant: sometimes the screen stayed empty for a long time, then filled almost at once. A high generation rate was compatible with an experience that felt slow.

To investigate, we separated two measurements. Time to first token starts when the request reaches our service and ends when the first output token becomes available. Output rate measures subsequent generation. Neither number alone describes an entire interaction. A user waiting for a short answer notices the initial pause; someone requesting a long report also notices the pace after it starts.

Our experiment compared two scheduler settings, called steady and split, on the same accelerator, model weights and maximum batch size. We replayed a fixed queue of 400 requests. Three hundred had short prompts; one hundred had a document attached. We used invented documents for this internal trial and fixed their token counts. Requests arrived at the same recorded times in both replays. We did not compare different model qualities or buy a larger machine for either setting.

Steady processed each new prompt's initial computation as a single block. Split divided that work into smaller blocks that could be interleaved with ongoing generation. The distinction matters when a long document arrives while other requests are already producing tokens. Those requests can wait behind the initial computation even if their own next token needs relatively little work. Dividing the work creates more opportunities to serve them, but managing those opportunities also has a cost.

For the short-prompt group, median time to first token was 180 milliseconds under steady and 150 under split. Its 95th percentile fell from 1,100 to 420 milliseconds. For the document group, the median moved the other way: from 620 to 710 milliseconds. Across the full replay, the aggregate output rate was 920 tokens per second for steady and 890 for split. These are results from this queue, not service guarantees. A percentile describes a distribution; the 95th-percentile change does not mean every request saved 680 milliseconds.

We also inspected a timeline instead of relying only on the summary table. The largest stalls clustered immediately after long prompts arrived. Split made those stalls less severe for short requests, while some long requests took longer to produce their first token. This pattern is consistent with sharing work more frequently. It does not show that the long documents became cheaper to process, or that the model generated fewer tokens to achieve the gain.

There are several boundaries on the result. The replay used one accelerator and one model. We did not run a saturation study across arrival rates, measure power consumption, or test a multi-machine deployment. The document requests had a narrower length distribution than production traffic. A queue made almost entirely of short prompts could behave differently because it offers less long initial work to divide.

The product team chose split for a small internal trial of the chat interface, where the empty-screen pause had been especially noticeable. The offline report generator will stay on steady for now: its users care more about total completion time and do not watch tokens arrive. Both choices use the same model. We have not changed the public service setting or announced a lower price.

The lesson is not that one scheduler wins. It is that measuring only throughput can hide a wait users actually experience. Before optimizing a dashboard number, we need to say whose wait the number represents, and what we are willing to trade to reduce it.
content_checks: Distinguish first-token delay from output rate and identify the scheduler trade-off.
Short-prompt p95 1100→420 ms; document median 620→710 ms; aggregate 920→890 tokens/s.
One fixed replay; no public rollout, price cut or general speed claim.

request: Make a practical explainer for technical writers joining this project.
context:
An error code should outlive its sentence
Engineering writing at Harbor Compiler

A year ago, our documentation linked to errors by quoting their full messages. That seemed reasonable because the compiler had fewer than thirty user-facing failures. When an engineer improved the wording of one message, however, a troubleshooting page stopped matching it. The software had become easier to understand in isolation and harder to search across the documentation.

We now assign a stable code to each class of error. The code describes a condition, not the exact sentence shown to a user. HC214, for example, means that a named module was found but does not export the requested member. Its message can mention the actual module and member, and its explanation can improve over time, without changing the identifier people use in reports.

Creating codes introduced a different temptation: giving every branch in the compiler a new number. We resisted that approach. Two internal paths that lead to the same user action can share a code. Conversely, a single internal exception may need separate codes if users must take different corrective steps. For a new writer, the best first task is to follow one code from a real failing example through its message and documentation. The places where those three disagree are usually more valuable than a fresh paragraph of general advice.
